name: Stories Made for One Classroom
title: Stories Made for One Classroom
answer: Teachers can use approved AI tools to create decodable stories and small custom activities that match the exact letter sounds, sight words and themes their class is learning. This solves the long-standing shortage of reading material pitched at the right level, and it lets young children become authors with their own dictated words. The teacher remains the checker and the decision maker, because AI output often breaks the phonics pattern or reads awkwardly.

sections.body: Early readers need stories built only from the letter sounds they have already learned, and these decodable stories have always been hard to find in enough variety. A teacher can ask an approved tool to write a short story using a set list of sounds and a few sight words, and can make it about the class pet or a recent field trip so children actually want to read it. The same method produces rhyming games, sound matching activities, counting scavenger hunts and circle time questions drawn from the week's theme. Activities that once took an evening to prepare now take a few minutes. The idea solves the mismatch between a published reading scheme and where a particular group of children actually is.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In preschool through second grade, a teacher picks the sounds and sight words the class has covered, asks an approved tool for a short story or activity, and checks it before printing. The story can feature familiar classroom details, which keeps children interested while the phonics load stays controlled. For authorship, a child dictates a story to the teacher, who uses a tool such as Canva for Education to turn it into an illustrated page, with the child's words kept as the child's words and AI helping only with pictures. The same request pattern works for five rhyming pairs from the week's theme or a counting hunt using objects already in the room. Teachers should watch closely which of these small custom activities children respond to.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book reports research on AI story building with young children, which found that it could work well at home, though children still preferred building stories with adults (Quan et al., 2026). For the wider set of small custom activities, the text states plainly that there is no study yet showing how much they help, so teachers should observe which ones children respond to. The book also notes from practice that AI tools often slip in words that break the phonics pattern, such as a long vowel sound the class has not learned, and can produce sentences that sound odd when read aloud. Figure 5.3 in the book lists a quick check a teacher can run in a few minutes before printing.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The teacher still has to check every story, because AI tools often include words that break the pattern, such as an unlearned long vowel sound, and can generate sentences that sound strange when read aloud. A short check, set out in Figure 5.3, is meant to be run before anything is printed. The child's words stay the child's words, and the AI only helps with the pictures, so authorship remains with the child. Because no study yet shows how much the small custom activities help, the judgement about which ones to keep using stays with the teacher, who watches how children respond.
